payload.description:
When install finishes in a repository that already excludes the managed core from its linters, I want it to say nothing, so I can stop training a consumer to skim the region where a tracked CI edit is also reported.

Found by the terminal canary, filed there as term-ip2wz and pressed after it shipped twice unchanged. scaffolds.install_notes tests only whether a config file exists, never what it contains, so it advises extend-exclude on a .ruff.toml that has carried exactly that for releases. The canary verified the exclusion is genuinely in force rather than merely present: ruff format --check over the managed core exits 0 on 54 files.

The same block tells a consumer to hand-edit .pre-commit-config.yaml in a run that separately reports it has just rewritten that file.

Severity is low and nothing fails. The reason it is worth fixing is where it sits: the advice is the tail of the install output, and the tail is also where a re-pin of a tracked CI workflow is announced. Unactionable boilerplate beside a real edit teaches a reader to skip both.

payload.description:
When an agent runs a positive control and it returns zero, I want the rule to say what the control must be built from, so I can stop reading a control's own zero as confirmation.

Asked for by the terminal canary as term-2vkce, and the request is well founded: the rule is in managed core they may never edit, they followed both halves of it, and still got a false reading. The wording said run a positive control and that if the control is empty too the zero belongs to the probe. It never said what the control must be built from.

Their case is the evidence. They planted a table they called ragged; it was valid compact style, so it was never a violation, reported zero, and read exactly like a dead probe. Rebuilt from the defect actually observed - padded cells over an unpadded delimiter row - it reported two errors. What rescued the diagnosis was the denominator: 151 files became 152 when the control was added, which proved the file was read and sent them to the table rather than the tooling.

Three of my own false zeros the same day were the environment answering instead of the code. Theirs is the subtler one and the one the rule did not cover.

Carrying it in their overlay was the fallback, and the objection to that is right: two copies of one rule drift, and ours is the copy every other consumer reads.
payload.requirements: the amendment sits in the existing bullet rather than adding one, because the always-on budget is a standing cost on every consumer. The token cost declared on the fragment is updated to what the projection measures rather than left to drift.
payload.title: amend the positive control rule with what a control must be built from

## Trigger

When a skill states a refusal that the code does not enforce, I want a gate to compare the claim against the flag tables, so I can stop a false claim from reaching a dispatched agent.

## The defect

The `work-tracker` skill carried **three** false statements at once (basicly-7wlhlp), each describing a refusal the code does not make. Every gate in the repository was green throughout. Skill prose is projected, linted for format, and checked for drift against its own source — and never checked against the behaviour it describes.

This is the population a green suite protects least: the consumer is a dispatched agent, so a false claim is not confusion, it is a lane that follows a wrong instruction and files no bug about it. One of the three told the reader that every labelling instruction is false, which would make an agent refuse `loop supervise --label`, the multi-lane path.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read `.basicly/core/skills/work-tracker/skill.yaml` before commit fbf844ba.
2. Note the Refuses section claims `update --add-label` raises, `create` without `--json` is refused, and the ready set is the open records.
3. Check each against `src/basicly/owned_write.py`, `src/basicly/tracker_write.py` and `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/differential.py`.
4. Run `uv run basicly verify --mode fast`, `uv run basicly skills-check --all-default-roots` and `uv run basicly catalog lint`.

Observed: all three claims are false, and every gate reports PASS.
Expected: a claim a skill makes about a refusal is checked against the table that implements it.

## The control that would have caught all three

Proposed by the lane that fixed them. `.scripts/docs_claims.py` already carries the mechanism: an `Assertion` that reads a catalog source and fails when it disagrees with an engine symbol. `_skill_work_types` is the working example, and `tests/test_docs_claims.py` has its anchor-vanished test.

Add an assertion that parses the skill's refusal section and fails when it names an `update` flag that `tracker_argv.UPDATE_LABEL_FLAGS` or `tracker_argv.UPDATE_FIELD_FLAGS` actually translates. That binds the prose to the tables whose change made it false, costs nothing per run, and is a deterministic gate rather than a judged one — which the standing constraints prefer.

## The scope question this raises, and does not answer

34 skills ship. This audited one. Whether the other 33 carry the same class of residue is **unmeasured**, and a per-skill hand audit does not scale. The generalisable form is: a skill that states a refusal names the symbol that implements it, and the gate checks the pair. That is a catalog-schema change, and it is larger than this record. Decide the narrow gate first and let its firing history argue for the general one.

## Scope

- `.scripts/docs_claims.py`
- `tests/test_docs_claims.py`

## Trigger

When the harness drives its full loop in a consumer repository, I want no third-party product to sit in the runtime path, so I can upgrade our own state on our own schedule.

## Context

**Corrected 2026-07-30 after the owner sharpened the criterion.** The first version of this epic
read the directive as "zero runtime dependencies" and set out to remove `jinja2`, `jsonschema`,
`pyyaml`, `rich`, `uv`, the pre-commit framework and node. That was wrong, and the correction
matters because it removes a large breaking change from the roadmap.

The axis is not external-versus-internal, nor binary-versus-package. It is:

> **Can we absorb this component's breaking change on our own schedule, or does it dictate terms
> to us?**

A **library or framework** is fine. It is versioned, we pin it, and when it ships a breaking
change we upgrade when ready and fix our own code. The blast radius is our source.

A **product** is not. `beads` is the case in point, and the evidence is already recorded in
`docs/design/work-tracker.md` section 2.10: crossing one of its schema migrations requires
*"exactly one designated clone"* to run `bd migrate` and `bd dolt push` while every other clone
installs the new binary and runs `bd bootstrap`. That is a coordinated, human-sequenced,
multi-machine operation sitting in our critical path. Worse, the upgrade is sometimes not
available at all: br's current main targets schema 17 and its reviewed migration accepts only
13-to-17 and 14-to-17, so a 0.2.19 database has no supported path forward from schema 16. A
dependency we cannot upgrade, and cannot decline to upgrade, is not a dependency we manage.

The compounding factor is that beads owns **our state** - every phase derivation, gate,
checkpoint, dependency edge, decision and run record. A library that owns no state can be swapped
in an afternoon; a product that owns the state cannot be swapped at all without a migration.

## The rule

**No third-party product may own basicly's state.** Libraries and frameworks are permitted and
pinned. An optional extension - existing skills, language or technology guidelines - is permitted
and must stay optional.

## Classification of every current dependency

| Component | Class | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jinja2`, `jsonschema`, `pyyaml`, `ruamel.yaml`, `rich` | library | **Keep.** Pinned, semver, owns no state. The catalog stays YAML - the stdlib-has-no-YAML-parser problem is no longer forcing a move to TOML. |
| `uv` | tool | **Keep.** Versioned, replaceable, owns no state. |
| pre-commit framework | framework | **Keep.** Dispatches our hooks; owns no state. |
| node (markdownlint hook) | tool | **Keep**, but it is the weakest entry - it is the only one whose absence has actually broken a commit path on this machine, and it earns a re-examination on its own merits rather than under this rule. |
| Python 3.14+ | language runtime | **Keep.** Not a product. Whether the floor should drop is an adoption question, not this one. |
| **`br` / beads** | **product that owns our state** | **Remove.** This is the whole of the directive. Tracked by `basicly-vkh0`. |
| **`bv`** | **product** | **Remove.** Measured at 0 of 141 surfaces used (`basicly-vkh0.2`), so this is a deletion rather than a replacement. |

## Why this epic still exists rather than folding into vkh0

`vkh0` removes the one product we have. This epic is the **policy** that stops the next one
arriving, which is the part that outlives the migration: the rule above written down where an
agent proposing a dependency will read it, the classification kept current, and a gate that
refuses a new runtime dependency it cannot classify.

## Success Criteria

- The dependency rule is stated in the architecture reference, every current dependency is classified against it, `br` and `bv` are gone from the runtime path, and a check refuses a newly added runtime dependency that is not classifiable as a library or framework

When a lane declares a scope glob that covers a configured append-only path, I want the preflight report to recognize that coverage the same way the landing does, so I can stop a false `contend:` line.

## Context

Found by the lane-B survey 2026-08-14.

```text
contention.py:61   path not in scopes.get(lane, ())     literal string membership
merge.py:942       merge._scope_covers                  decompose.globs_overlap
```

So a lane that declares `docs/**` or `*.md` covers a configured append-only `CHANGELOG.md` at the landing, and the preflight counts it as a lane that contends without declaring.

## Why it matters despite being advisory

Nothing refuses on this surface. The cost is a false `contend:` line. This repository records that an advisory `contend:` line is a finding an operator acts on: one such line named the exact collision under a green verdict and four hand-resolved rebases followed. A false one spends the same attention.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the two scope tests side by side:

       rg -n 'path not in scopes.get' src/basicly/contention.py
       rg -n -A8 'def _scope_covers' src/basicly/merge.py

   `contention.append_only_report` asks `path not in scopes.get(lane, ())` - literal string
   membership against the lane's declared entries. `merge._scope_covers` asks
   `decompose.globs_overlap(path, glob)`. A lane declaring `docs/**` or `*.md` satisfies the
   second and fails the first.
2. Note the report is inert on this repo as configured, so the case has to supply a path:

       rg -n '^append_only_paths' basicly.toml

   Observed 2026-08-19: `append_only_paths = []`, and `append_only_report` returns its

   test. So the reproduction belongs in `tests/test_contention.py` against a fixture repo
   that configures `append_only_paths = ["CHANGELOG.md"]`, not against this checkout.
3. In that fixture, give two lanes a `## Scope`: one declaring the glob `*.md` on its own
   backticked line, one declaring nothing that covers `CHANGELOG.md`. Call
   `contention.append_only_report` with both lanes.

## Trigger

When feature pressure adds work faster than a one-off architecture audit can track, I want a mechanism that drains the backlog and bounds the whole tree, so I can stop the review from becoming a second unmanaged backlog.

## Goal

Cut unnecessary complexity, dead code and ambiguous concepts out of basicly, and leave behind the deterministic and non-deterministic mechanisms that make a one-off pass unnecessary ever again.

## Why the mechanism half is not optional

**This analysis has already been run once.** `basicly-tcmy` is the 2026-08-01 architecture and code review: three read-only passes over the engine, the projector and the instruction catalog. Its own baseline reads *43 modules in a six-tier DAG*. Measured 2026-08-14: **86 modules, 42,966 lines**, and **13 of its children are still open**.

So a read-only pass that emits a prioritised list is a thing this repo can already produce. What it cannot do is **drain the list against feature pressure**. Commissioning a second audit without the draining mechanism buys a second backlog with the same fate, which is why pass 2 below is a precondition of the work being worth paying for rather than a follow-on.

The supporting measurement: `src/basicly/` went **36,641 to 42,966 lines in one week** with the module-size ratchet, the comment-density ratchet, the noqa ratchet, vulture, lint-imports and wired-or-deleted all live and green. **A ratchet bounds a file. Nothing bounds the tree.**

## The three passes

**Pass 0 - re-verify the inherited backlog.** Take `basicly-tcmy`'s 13 open children against today's tree and classify each done, moot, still-real or worse, with the check that decides it. A finding cites a `path:line` and code moves; an unverified inherited finding is a claim, not evidence. Adding new findings on top of an unverified backlog is how you get two backlogs.

**Pass 1 - the survey.** The `architect` role, at its declared maximum tier, over the tree. Output is a dependency-ordered backlog shaped so the plan gate admits it unchanged, so the loop can dispatch it without translation.

Scope exclusions, each with a reason rather than an exemption:

- `br.py` and the 32 `run_br` call sites across 12 modules - they leave the tree at the tracker flip (`basicly-u4xu`). Auditing a scheduled deletion spends budget the calendar already spends.
- `runner.py`'s subprocess dispatch path - replaced by `basicly-xjd2`.
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/` - no frozen surface, no declared schema, no cache decision. An audit needs a specification to judge against, and `work-tracker.md` section 7 now records that one does not exist.

**Pass 2 - the mechanisms.** Deterministic and non-deterministic, both, because each covers what the other cannot: a gate binds without judgement and cannot read intent; a role judges and cannot bind.

Non-deterministic, all already specified and none of them new inventions:

- `basicly-feje` - map `reviewer` to a phase so the per-lens adversarial review runs on every lane instead of never.
- `basicly-u2hl.22` - derive `change-shape` from an AST. This is the call-chain instrument; without it "a call chain that does not make sense" is a thing only a human notices.
- RETROSPECTIVE as a state with the special-cause trigger, so the system decides *when* a structural finding is worth acting on instead of tampering on every single occurrence.

Deterministic:

- `basicly-u2hl.27` - the controller and actuator. Set point, four sensors and the dampener already exist; what is missing is the thing that selects the next target and dispatches it. **This is the bead that decides whether any of the rest lands.**
- A tree-level size budget, because the per-file ratchets were all green through a 17%-in-one-week growth.
- `basicly-r343` - the dead-code gate reads English prose in a schema as a field reference, so it can pass a real finding.
- `basicly-plhx` - the agent schema lets a role ship with no tier, so D26's routing rule can be defeated silently.
- `basicly-a3yi` - resolve a declared tier into the projected surface, so a tier declaration reaches a spawn at all.

## Ranking rule for the backlog

Dependency order, not severity order. Severity decides what is in; dependency decides what is next. The finding that unblocks the most other findings goes first.

## Trigger

When two lanes each change a declared generated block by the same amount, I want the block to rebuild from the merged tree on every landing, so I can stop a clean auto-merge from leaving a silently wrong count.

## Context

Found 2026-08-14 when lane `basicly-2j5a` bounced on `docs-claims` at its landing, hours after
`basicly-3w51` shipped the per-path rebuild that exists to prevent exactly that bounce.

The rebuild is triggered by a **rebase conflict**. Two lanes that each increment the same counter to
the same value produce **identical text**, so git auto-merges them cleanly, no conflict is raised, the
rebuild never fires, and the merged value is wrong by one.

Observed, not reasoned:

```text
base after basicly-3oxp landed          Test files | 163
lane basicly-2j5a's own block            Test files | 163   (correct in its pre-rebase tree)
after the rebase, no conflict raised     Test files | 163
the true value with both files present               164
```

The landing then failed on `docs-claims`, and regenerating in the rebased worktree produced 164.

## What worked and what did not, stated separately

**The gate failed safe.** `docs-claims` refused the landing rather than committing a false count, which
is the behaviour that matters most. Nothing wrong reached main.

**The mechanism did not do its job.** `basicly-3w51` exists so a lane does not bounce on a file it did
not author. Here the lane bounced anyway, and a human had to regenerate the block by hand and commit
it. That is the cost `3w51` was bought to remove, and it returns for every pair of lanes that move a
counter by the same amount - which for a counter incremented by one is the *common* case, not the rare
one.

## Why the conflict trigger is the wrong predicate

A conflict means the two sides disagree textually. What a generated block actually needs is a
rebuild whenever **its inputs changed**, and its inputs are the tree, not the file. Two lanes each
adding one test file change the input twice while writing the same text once.

So the predicate wants to be *the path is declared generated and this landing touched anything its
command reads*, or more simply: rebuild a declared generated path on every landing, unconditionally.
The command is deterministic and cheap - `docs_claims.py --fix --block` runs in well under a second -
so an unconditional rebuild costs almost nothing and removes a whole class of near-miss.

Note the tension to resolve rather than assume: `3w51` deliberately scoped the rebuild to conflicts
because the file is only **partly** generated and discarding both sides of the whole path would
destroy hand-authored prose. An unconditional rebuild must therefore stay block-scoped, which
`--block` already makes possible. That is why this is filed as a change to the trigger and not to the
resolution.

## Acceptance

- When a landing rebases a lane that changed a declared generated path, then the path is rebuilt from
  the merged tree regardless of whether the rebase raised a conflict.
- When two lanes each add one test file and land in sequence, then the second landing produces the
  true count without a human regenerating anything.
- When a rebuild runs, then hand-authored prose outside the marked block is unchanged, asserted
  against a lane that edited both.
- When the rebuild command fails or leaves a conflict marker, then the landing still bounces to the
  lane, as it does today.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/rebase.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_rebase.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Warning

`tests/test_rebase.py` sits at exactly the 4000-token cap with zero headroom and is unfrozen -
`basicly-e2mz.2` is filed against precisely that. Sequence this after it, or expect the gate to refuse
the first line you add.

Land two lanes that each add one test file, in sequence, with no human intervention between them, and
read the generated block on main: it must equal the tree. Then land a lane that edits the
hand-authored prose beside the block and confirm the edit survives.

## Trigger

When the supervisor selects more lanes than it provisions, I want the pass to name the withheld lane and the rule that withheld it, so I can tell a deliberate refusal from a defect.

## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run basicly loop supervise basicly-u2hl --label u2hl-pass-2
rg "^(wip|routed):" <the pass log>
```

Observed, two passes on 2026-08-15:

```
pass 1  wip: 0/5 unlanded downstream of build; 2 lane(s) admitted
        routed: provisioned 2 of 3 lane(s) selected by label
pass 2  wip: 0/5 unlanded downstream of build; 1 lane(s) admitted
        routed: provisioned 1 of 2 lane(s) selected by label
```

Both passes had **zero** work in flight against a headroom of five, and both left a
selected lane unprovisioned with no line saying why. Pass 2 then provisioned the
remaining lane on a later tick, after the first had shipped - so the two lanes ran
serially despite disjoint declared scopes and a wholly empty WIP bound.

Expected - when a selected lane is not provisioned, the pass says which lane and on
what rule.

## Why this is worth a bead rather than a shrug

The visible cost is throughput: pass 2 was two lanes with no scope overlap and it ran
them one after the other, so the pass took the sum rather than the maximum.

The invisible cost is worse and it is what happened here. A reader who sees
"provisioned 1 of 2" cannot tell a deliberate refusal from a defect, so the first
reading of pass 1 attributed it to `basicly-0p8n` being a `feature` and therefore not
a leaf track - which was true of that bead and does not explain pass 2, where both
`ho3t` and `u2hl.30` are leaf types with a readable `## Scope`. One plausible cause
was tested and refuted: `br blocked` does **not** propagate a blocked parent to its
children - measured, 45 entries against 32 with a real open blocks-edge, and every one
of the 13 extra is an epic with open children, with zero false negatives. So the cause
is still unknown, and that is the point.

`wip.py:169` admits `ready[:headroom]`, so the remainder is upstream of the WIP bound
in whatever produces `ready`. The line already prints on the admitted path
deliberately (`wip.py:105`); it needs to print on the withheld one too.

- `src/basicly/wip.py`

  deliberate refusal is distinguishable from a defect.
- Given the WIP bound withheld a lane when the pass reports then `wip.WipAdmission.coverage`
  prints the withheld ids on the *withheld* path, as it already does on the admitted one.

## Trigger

When a module sits exactly at the size cap with no freeze, I want the gate to report its headroom, so I can split it before it blocks the next lane that touches it.

## Context

Reported by the `basicly-3w51` lane 2026-08-14 and confirmed by hand at main after the merge.

```text
tests/test_rebase.py    tokens=4000   cap=4000   headroom=0
```

The module-size gate reports PASS, because 4000 is within the 4000-token cap. It is at the cap
exactly, and it is **not frozen** — so there is no baseline to fall back on. The next line added to
that file fails `module-size` outright, and the failure lands on whoever touches `rebase` next
rather than on whoever filled it.

## Why this is not the ordinary ratchet obligation

A frozen module above the cap may only shrink, and the first touch below 2x the cap must bring it
under. Both rules give the next author a payable move. A file resting on the cap with no freeze
gives none: it is green today and red on the next character, with nothing in the gate output saying
so. `module-size` prints a count of modules within cap or baseline; it does not print headroom, so a
file at zero is indistinguishable from one at two thousand.

Two separable pieces of work, and the second is the one that generalises.

## Acceptance

- When `tests/test_rebase.py` is split along a nameable responsibility, then each part is under the
  cap with room to add a test, and no assertion or fixture is deleted to buy the room.
- When `module-size` runs, then it names any tracked module whose headroom against its cap or its
  frozen baseline is below a declared threshold, so a file about to block the next lane is visible
  before it blocks one.
- When the headroom report exists, then it reports rather than blocks, because it has no firing
  history yet.

## Scope

- `tests/test_rebase.py`
- a new test module under `tests/`
- `.scripts/check_module_size.py`
- `tests/test_check_module_size.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run python .scripts/check_module_size.py` prints a headroom line naming every module below the
threshold, and adding one assertion to each split part of `tests/test_rebase.py` passes the gate.

## Note on the population this belongs to

Measured at main on 2026-08-14, three other modules sit at or near zero: `tests/test_decompose.py`
0 against a frozen 28885, `src/basicly/policy.py` 9 against 32482, `src/basicly/decompose.py` 11
against 24498. Two lanes in this session each had to cut their own added prose to land, and one
moved its regression test to a different file because the natural home had 1 token free. That is the
recurring shape, not a single file.

When code is inserted above a cited symbol, I want the citation to name the symbol rather than its line, so I can stop an unrelated edit from invalidating a true claim.

## Context

Filed 2026-08-15 after the gate `basicly-miqr` shipped that morning fired four times in
one afternoon, on one changeset, all from the same cause.

## Observed

A single change adding 18 lines to `src/basicly/loop.py` invalidated **20 citations** across
`docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` and `docs/requirements/factory-loop.md`. Trimming a
docstring in the same file later moved two of them back and invalidated two more. None of

`check_docs_citations.py` already resolves the symbol - its own failure text reads
`outside the symbol named here - `foreign_dirt` is at :509`. So it knows the answer it is
asking the author to write down. A `file.py:line` citation is a claim that decays on every
insertion above it, while `file.py::symbol` would not.

the reason to remove the need for the fixer rather than to improve it.

The one real correction found in the same afternoon is the argument for keeping it: the plan

entirely. A symbol-form citation would have failed on the missing symbol rather than

## Trigger

When a tracked file changes during a failing commit gate because of a concurrent writer, I want `basicly commit` to name that file as concurrently modified, so I can stop losing time chasing the wrong hook.

## Context

`pre-commit` snapshots the working tree before each hook and compares it after. A file
that changed during a hook is reported as **modified by that hook**. A concurrent
writer is indistinguishable from a hook write, so the blame lands on whichever hook was
running when the write arrived.

Measured 2026-08-16. Three commits in a row failed with
`catalog-lint: files were modified by this hook`, while `catalog lint: OK` printed in
the same output. A whole-tree probe cleared the command:

```
git ls-files -z | xargs -0 md5sum | sort > before
uv run basicly catalog lint
git ls-files -z | xargs -0 md5sum | sort > after
diff before after   ->  no output
```

The real writer was a background agent editing `docs/architecture/architecture.md`.
Its diff went from 416 to 528 insertions between the second and third attempts, so it
wrote inside the commit window. An hour went into the wrong hook.

## Why the framework cannot answer this and we can

`pre-commit` has no way to tell a hook's write from anybody else's, and it is not ours
to change. `basicly commit` already wraps `git commit`, so it is the one place that can
snapshot the tracked tree before the gate and compare after a failure. A file that
changed but is touched by no hook is a concurrent modification, and saying so turns an
hour of hunting into one line.

Post-hoc diagnosis on failure only. Not a refusal, and not a pre-flight heuristic on
file age - a human editing in another window is a false positive, and a gate that cries
wolf gets waived.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Stage a commit in this repo and start it through the wrapper:

       uv run basicly commit ...

2. While the gate is running, have a second process write to any tracked file the commit
   does not touch - for example append a line to `docs/architecture/architecture.md`.
3. Read the failure. `pre-commit` snapshots the tree before each hook and compares it
   after, so it reports `<hook-id>: files were modified by this hook` naming whichever hook
   happened to be running when the write arrived.
4. Clear the named hook by hand, which is the step that costs the time:

       git ls-files -z | xargs -0 md5sum | sort > before
       uv run basicly catalog lint
       git ls-files -z | xargs -0 md5sum | sort > after
       diff before after

5. Probe `basicly commit` for anything that would have said so:

       rg -n 'concurrent' src/basicly/commit.py tests/test_commit.py
       rg -c 'hook' src/basicly/commit.py

Observed - this record's measurement 2026-08-16: three commits in a row failed with
`catalog-lint: files were modified by this hook` while `catalog lint: OK` printed in the same
output, step 4's `diff` produced no output, and the real writer was a background agent whose
diff on `architecture.md` grew from 416 to 528 insertions between the second and third
attempts. An hour went into the wrong hook. Step 5, re-run 2026-08-19: the first command
returns nothing. **Its positive control is the second command**, which returns 15 `hook`
matches in a 586-line `commit.py`, and `grep -c 'def test_' tests/test_commit.py` returns 35
- both files exist and are searched, so the zero is an absence.

Expected: when a tracked file changed during a failing gate and no hook is configured to
touch it, `basicly commit` names that file as concurrently modified, post-hoc and on failure
only. When nothing changed, it says nothing about concurrency.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/commit.py`
- `tests/test_commit.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/commit.py`
- `tests/test_commit.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_commit.py -k concurrent -q`

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- Given a tracked file changes while the commit gate runs when the commit fails then

  blamed - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_commit.py -k concurrent -q`
- Given no file changes during a failing gate then the output says nothing about
  concurrency - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_commit.py -k concurrent -q`

When an operator failure repeats because no gate refused it, I want the remedy to be a deterministic check rather than added prose, so I can stop the next lane from hitting the same wall.

## Context

On 2026-08-16 every lane failure in the session was operator error, not an engine defect. The engine refused correctly and named the cause every time. The owner asked for a remedy, and the remedy is not simply more prose in the always-on files.

This repository already states the hierarchy: git hooks are the deterministic floor, and guidance is what you use when a gate cannot express the check. The always-on baseline is also measured at 7014 to 7343 characters and is at its cap, so a new always-on rule costs something real and must earn it.

## The four failures and the tier each one belongs in

1. A stray 7.6 MB file under the tracker directory was committed by the tracker-state rollup, which stages the whole directory. CODE. Filed as basicly-vkh0.31.

Run after the architecture rewrite is verified and swapped in. The rewrite renumbers sections that code cites, and doing both at once would tangle two unrelated diffs.

- `tests/**`

## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-16. `basicly-vkh0.32` was refused at the landing:

    [blocked] build -> build: basicly-vkh0.32 changed .importlinter, docs/plan/implementation-plan.md,
    src/basicly/br.py, src/basicly/edge_adoption.py, tests/test_edge_adoption.py,
    tests/test_tracker_cutover.py outside its declared scope
    (src/basicly/tracker_cutover.py, tests/test_tracker_adoption.py), and basicly-b2n2 declared
    that ground: the plan is wrong, not the merge.

Half of that refusal was correct and is not this bead: the scope declaration really was wrong, and the gate said so precisely.

The other half was a collision with a lane that had produced nothing:

    git log --oneline main..harness/basicly-b2n2 | wc -l    -> 0
    git -C <worktree> status --short | wc -l                -> 0

Zero commits ahead of main, clean worktree, sitting on a base from an earlier session. `basicly-b2n2` had held `src/basicly/br.py` and a worktree slot since before the session while writing no code.

Tearing the worktree down released the ground and the lane landed. Nothing was lost, because there was nothing to lose.

## The gap

The architecture defines live deliberately: "Live means the worktree session records on disk, not the tracker export." The reason is good and should not be reverted - a freshly provisioned lane is the one most likely to be mid-edit, and the export would not show it.

But presence of a worktree record is a weak proxy for occupancy. It cannot distinguish:

- a lane mid-edit with uncommitted work, which must hold its ground;
- a lane with commits, which must hold its ground;
- a lane with no commits and a clean tree, which is holding a claim and a concurrency slot and nothing else.

The third case cost a landing, a rework attempt, and an operator decision today. It also occupied one of five worktree slots, which separately blocked a dispatch earlier in the same session.

## What this is not

Not an argument for reading the tracker export instead. Not an argument for auto-reaping a lane: a human parked it for a reason, and deleting work is the one thing a scope gate must never do. A lane with no commits but a dirty tree is genuinely mid-edit and must keep its ground.

The remedy is discrimination and a better message, not eviction.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/contention.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

| Population | Count |
| --- | --- |
| acceptance criteria in the structured field | 134 |
| field empty, but the description carries an `## Acceptance Criteria` heading | 32 |
| criteria nowhere at all | **55**, of which 52 are not epics |

The discriminator is proven rather than assumed, with one probe per population:

    basicly policy dor basicly-vkh0.36   ->  DoR: READY          (field populated)
    basicly policy dor basicly-e2mz.35   ->  DoR: READY          (heading in the description only)
    basicly policy dor basicly-y8el      ->  DoR: NOT READY - missing: ## Acceptance Criteria

Two reasons, and the second is the one that makes it a mechanism problem.

A dispatch on any of the 55 costs a worktree provisioning and an intake advance before the refusal, so the cost of the gap is paid per attempt rather than once.

A report that names every open record the readiness check refuses, with the reason it gives, so the gap is one command rather than 221 probes. It reads the live check rather than re-implementing its rules.

## Trigger

When the decompose proposer prompt states the shared-scope rule backward and gives no rule for a child's type, I want the prompt corrected to match the plan validator and the harness-loop skill, so I can stop plans being refused or a leaf-shaped child typed as a feature.

## Context

Found 2026-08-07 by exercising `basicly-u6jq.2` on live work, hours after it landed. The
delegated decompose proposer is dispatched, produces a plan, and the plan is then refused or
lands a child that cannot be built - **because the prompt does not carry rules the
`harness-loop` skill states**. Two instances, same root cause.

Both are cheap to fix and both convert a delegated phase back into a human stop, which is the
exact thing the dark factory exists to remove.

## Steps to Reproduce

### Instance 1 - `shared` prose contradicts the output contract

1. Take a bead whose scope includes a shared anchor (a README or an architecture status
   table). `basicly-imnu.2` is one.
2. Run `basicly loop run basicly-imnu.2 --work-type feature --root basicly-imnu.2`.

Observed:

```
[blocked] classify -> classify: decompose needs an agent-proposed child plan; the proposed
child plan failed the plan schema: children[0] 'shared' entry
'docs/architecture/architecture.md' is not in that child's 'scope'; declare the path in
'scope' too, so the recorded scope stays the whole truth (needs input: children)
```

Expected: the plan validates, or the proposer is told the rule it must satisfy.

The cause is a contradiction inside one prompt in `src/basicly/loop.py`, about seven lines
apart. The prose:

> list under 'shared' any literal path the child touches **but does not own**

The output contract immediately below it:

> `"shared": ["<literal path already in scope>", ...]`

These say opposite things. A path a child "does not own" is precisely a path not in its
`scope`, and the validator enforces the second reading - `shared` must be a subset of
`scope`. A proposer that follows the prose, which is stated first and in natural language,
is refused every time.

`.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml` has it right: "also list in `shared` any
literal path **from its `scope`** the child only appends its own entry to". The prompt's
prose diverged from the skill it implements.

### Instance 2 - the proposer types a leaf-shaped child as `feature`

1. Run the same proposer against `basicly-3ifz`.
2. It produced `basicly-3ifz.1` - a good plan, five well-formed acceptance criteria, correct
   scope - typed **`feature`**.

Observed: `basicly-3ifz.1` is a single coherent change (one new module, one CLI subcommand,
two test files) and a `feature` blocks at decompose demanding a child plan of its own,
provisioning no worktree. It had to be retyped by hand to `task` before it could be built.

Expected: the proposer classifies a child by shape.

The cause is that the prompt states the enum, `"type": "<bug|chore|task|feature>"`, and gives
no rule for choosing. The skill does give the rule: "classify by shape, not by ambition: one
coherent change is a `task`, and only work that genuinely fans out into separately landable
children is a `feature`. A `feature` blocks at decompose demanding a child plan and
provisions no worktree, so a leaf-shaped bead filed as one stalls before any code is
written."

## Cost

Measured this session: two proposer dispatches at 64,789 and 69,082 tokens. Cheap per
occurrence, but instance 1 blocks the lane outright and instance 2 lands a child that stalls
on its first dispatch. A shared anchor is the common case for a fan-out, not the rare one.

## Fix

Carry both rules into the prompt from the skill that already states them. For instance 1
correct the prose - it is the wrong half. **Do not relax the validator**, which is right for
the reason its own message gives: the recorded scope has to stay the whole truth, and a
`shared` path outside `scope` is a file the child writes without declaring.

Add a regression test that the prompt and the plan validator agree on the subset rule. A
contradiction between two strings in one prompt is caught by no existing gate, which is why
this reached live work.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

payload.value: The prompt SHALL state the shared-is-a-subset-of-scope rule exactly once, in the direction the plan validator enforces. The prompt SHALL carry the classify-by-shape rule for choosing a child's type. A test SHALL fail if the prompt and the plan validator disagree on either rule.

## Trigger

When a hook declared manager claude has a copilot equivalent stage but Copilot only receives the telemetry hook, I want protect-generated projected to Copilot too, so I can gate the two agent families alike before the git floor has to catch it later.

## Context

Agent hooks are projected per family by `hooks.yaml`'s `manager` field, and the two
families are **not** at parity [M 2026-08-08]:

```text
manager: claude    protect-generated      stage=pretooluse
manager: claude    tool-usage             stage=posttooluse
manager: copilot   tool-usage-copilot     stage=posttooluse
```

So a consumer on Copilot gets the telemetry hook and **not the guard**.
`protect-generated` refuses an edit to a generated file at tool time; on Copilot that
edit is caught only later, by the `protect-generated-commit` git hook. The git floor
still holds, so nothing is unsafe — but the earlier refusal, which is the whole point
of an agent hook (`factory-loop.md` section 3.3: source inspection beats successive),
is Claude-only.

## The premise that blocked this, and why it is gone

The repo believed Copilot had **no hook surface at all**. That claim was recorded in the
tier kit and repeated into `architecture.md`, and it was **wrong** — an artifact of a
probe that looked for a `hooks/` directory under `~/.copilot`, a hook key in a
`settings.json` that simply had none set, and a `--help` that does not enumerate config
keys. None of the three was a positive control.

Corrected and fetched from the vendor 2026-08-08:

```text
config          .github/hooks/*.json  |  settings.json "hooks"  |  config.json "hooks"
                config.json "disableAllHooks" turns them all off
events          sessionStart  sessionEnd  userPromptSubmitted
                preToolUse  postToolUse  errorOccurred
preToolUse      documented as able to APPROVE or DENY a tool call
```

`preToolUse` approving or denying is exactly what `protect-generated` needs, so this is
extension rather than invention — the projection layer already routes by `manager` and
already writes a managed `.github/hooks/basicly-<id>.json`.

## What this bead is NOT

**It does not resolve tier injection.** That needs a hook to *modify* a spawn's
arguments, not to approve or deny one, and no copilot hook has been shown to fire for an
agent spawn at all (three probes on 1.0.77, `basicly-wbsz`). Approve/deny and modify are
different capabilities; keep them apart. The tier kit's static fallback stands until
someone demonstrates a spawn-time rewrite.

## Constraints

- **The git hooks remain the deterministic floor.** An agent hook is an earlier surface,
  never a replacement — a consumer on a host without one must still get the same
  guarantee at commit time.
- **Parity is a claim on a consumer surface, so it must be exercised, not asserted.**
  `basicly-irrm` already caught this shape once when the README advertised three agents
  and the ledger held dispatches for one. A projected hook that never fires is the
  instrument-built-and-never-connected defect this repo keeps rediscovering.
- Event names are the vendor's and change without our involvement; treat the mapping
  from `stage` to a copilot event as data, re-probed rather than recalled.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly hooks-build && uv run basicly hooks-check` writes and verifies a copilot
`preToolUse` guard, and `ls .github/hooks/` shows it beside the existing telemetry hook.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/hooks.yaml`
- `src/basicly/hooks.py`
- `tests/test_hooks.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `90000`
- depends on: none

  when the projection runs, then an equivalent copilot hook is written - check: a test
  asserts `protect-generated` produces a `.github/hooks/` entry on `preToolUse`.
- Given the projected copilot guard, when an agent edits a generated file, then the edit
  is refused before it lands - check: drive the hook with a real `preToolUse` payload
  naming a generated path and assert the deny response; and exercise it in a live
  session, since a projected hook that never fires is the defect this bead exists to
  avoid.
- Given a stage with no copilot equivalent, when the projection runs, then it declines
  and says why rather than writing a hook that cannot fire - check: a test asserts the
  decline path and its message.

The original record named four files and **all four are gone**: the engine module for the retired binary, a tracker surface module, and their two tests. The code moved, so the record read as stale. The concern is not stale, and the shape has changed.

**The correct fix already exists.** `src/basicly/checkout.py` line 76 defines a shared wrapper that passes `encoding="utf-8"` explicitly, and its docstring names the reason: Windows defaults to cp1252. `checkout.git` routes every git call through it. That half is done and should not be re-done.

## Trigger

When a rework round trades one finding for another and the verdict logic calls that progressing while the parent bead's own context sentence calls it a stall, I want the disagreement decided from the finding-set ledger telemetry, so I can either change the comparison threshold or correct the context sentence.

## Context

Found 2026-08-06 by exercising `basicly-m4zv.5` from base after it merged, rather than by
reading its tests. The landed behaviour satisfies the acceptance criterion and contradicts
one sentence of the same bead's Context, so the AC passing hid a design question.

`basicly-m4zv.5`'s Context says:

> Compare the open-finding set between consecutive iterations, not the count - **a round that
> fixes one finding and introduces one is not progress.**

The landed implementation disagrees. Measured against base at 4cbc777:

```
history [{pytest, ruff}]  now {pytest, vulture}
  verdict=progressing  rounds=0  -> keep spending
```

`policy._compare_finding_sets` returns `STALLED` only on set identity and `DIVERGING` only on a
strict superset; everything else is `PROGRESSING`. A trade is neither, so it falls through and
the round keeps spending its cap. There is a test asserting exactly this -
`test_a_finding_set_that_traded_one_finding_for_another_is_progressing` - so it is a decision,
not an oversight.

## Which is right is genuinely open

The AC only ever defined three cases - unchanged once, unchanged twice, grows - and a trade is
none of them, so **the implementation is correct against the AC**. The question is whether the
AC was complete.

**For the landed behaviour (trade = progressing).** Fixing `ruff` while `vulture` newly fails is
real movement, and a lane that clears findings one per round is the normal shape of iterative
work. Escalating it would ask a human about a lane that is working, and at `[policy] max_rework
= 2` there is almost no room for a lane to be wrong once. The rework cap already bounds a lane
that thrashes forever, so nothing is unbounded either way.

**For the Context sentence (trade = stalled).** The count is unchanged and the *quality* is
unknown; a lane that trades a finding every round never converges and burns its whole cap
before the cap notices. That is the same failure this bead's parent exists to stop, one level
subtler.

**A third reading, which may be what the sentence meant.** The sentence's job may be to argue
against comparing *counts* - "a count cannot tell a trade from real progress, so compare sets" -
rather than to fix the verdict for a trade. Under that reading nothing is wrong and this bead
closes as already-satisfied with the sentence clarified.

## What would settle it

Telemetry, not argument. `policy.record_finding_set` now writes a `[harness-policy] finding-set`
marker on every rework round, so the data accrues from here on: count how often consecutive
rounds trade rather than shrink, and whether those lanes eventually landed or escalated. A trade
that usually precedes a landing is progress; one that usually precedes an escalation is a stall.
Decide from the ledger the way `basicly-m4zv.14` settled the `-n auto` question, and do not
change the threshold before the ledger has entries.

## Steps to Reproduce

```sh
uv run python -c "
from basicly import policy
A = policy.finding_signature(['pytest','ruff'])
B = policy.finding_signature(['pytest','vulture'])
print(policy._compare_finding_sets([A], B))"
```

Prints `('progressing', ('pytest','ruff'), 0)`. Expected, if the Context sentence governs, is a
stalled verdict.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The trade rate between consecutive rework rounds and the eventual landing or escalation outcome of those lanes shall be counted from the ledger's `[harness-policy] finding-set` markers. A decision shall be recorded on whether a traded finding set counts as stalled or as progress, backed by that count. Either `policy._compare_finding_sets` shall change with tests, or the `basicly-m4zv.5` context sentence shall be corrected to match the landed behaviour.

## Trigger

When a pre-push run buffers every check's progress marker until the whole gate finishes, I want progress to stream as each check runs, so I can tell a slow gate from a wedged one without waiting the full duration.

## Measured

A complete pre-push run took **852s (~14 minutes)**, of which pytest was **798s**. It re-runs
gates that already passed at commit time: ruff, ruff-format, pyright x3, bandit, vulture,
wired-or-deleted, lint-imports, pytest, four projection checks and docs-claims.

A second attempt was abandoned after 11 minutes because another repository's quality gates were
running concurrently on the same machine - its `pip_audit` is network-bound - and the two
workloads competed for cores. Nothing was wrong with either; the machine was oversubscribed.
Recorded so the 852s figure is not read as a clean single-tenant measurement.

## Two consequences, and the second is the one to fix first

**A fourteen-minute push is a bypass generator.** This repo forbids `--no-verify`, which is the
right rule, and a gate this slow puts pressure on it anyway. A rule that depends on patience is
a rule with a half-life. Decide deliberately what genuinely must run pre-push versus what CI is
the correct floor for - the four projection checks and docs-claims are deterministic and cheap,
pytest at 798s is the whole cost.

**`pre-commit` buffers hook output until the hook exits**, so a long pre-push shows a bare
`pre-push-script....` line for its entire duration and is indistinguishable from a hang. That is
a **diagnosability** defect independent of the duration, it is cheaper to fix than the runtime,
and it is what makes the runtime feel like a failure. An operator who cannot tell a slow gate
from a wedged one will eventually kill one that was working.

## Constraint on any fix

Do not weaken the gate to make it fast. The repo rule is explicit: never defeat a gate to force
success. Splitting work between pre-push and CI is a **relocation** of the floor and must leave
the floor intact - anything moved to CI must actually block the merge there, or this becomes a
quiet removal.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/pre-push.py`
- `basicly.toml`
- `.github/workflows/`

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The pre-push hook shall flush each check's progress marker immediately, so progress is visible while the gate still runs. Any check relocated from pre-push to CI shall still block the merge in CI, so the floor is relocated rather than removed.

## Trigger

When work is running that the board's `running now` region cannot see, I want the region to name only the population it actually draws, so I can trust it will not imply it is showing everything.

## Context

Owner question, 2026-08-22: *"I also understand that the only things that are shown on the board are the ones started by supervisor. what about other subagents or background agents - are they also shown on the board?"*

The answer is **no**, and it is structural rather than an omission in the producer.

## Measured

A board lane comes from one place: `board_facts.lane_facts` calls `supervise.derive_session(...)` and reads `state.adopted` (`src/basicly/board_facts.py:237-238`). An `AdoptedLane` (`src/basicly/supervise.py:466-474`) is *"one in-flight lane re-adopted from its br worktree binding"* and carries a required `loop_state.WorktreeBinding`.

So a thing appears on the board if and only if it has **a tracker record carrying a `worktree:` external_ref**. A subagent spawned through a host's own agent tool has neither. A background shell job has neither.

`rg -n 'subagent|sub-agent|background|spawn' src/basicly/board_*.py` returns two hits and both are prose in unrelated docstrings, saying the producer *spawns* nothing. Positive control: `rg -c 'lane' src/basicly/board_facts.py` returns 30, so the probe reaches the files and the absence is real.

## Why this matters more than it looks

The region is headed `RUNNING NOW`. A reader takes that as *what is happening in this repository*, and on 2026-08-22 the true answer included four read-only investigation subagents and two background shell jobs that the board could not see and did not mention. The heading over-claims: it means *what the supervisor dispatched*, and nothing says so.

That is the same class as `basicly-a68ggd`, where a region headed `THE LOOP` shows the whole backlog. A heading that names more than its producer can see is a defect whichever direction the gap runs.

## What is genuinely hard here

A subagent is **not** a lane and should not be drawn as one. It has no tracker record, no worktree, no branch, no acceptance criteria, and no landing. Giving it a lane card would invite a reader to expect a merge that will never come.

It also may not be observable at all. A lane is a subprocess this engine spawned and metered, so its stream is readable; a subagent of the *host* is inside the host's own process tree and the engine has no handle on it. Whether it can be counted at all is the first question this record has to answer rather than assume - and if the answer is that it cannot, then the honest fix is the heading and not a new section.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_regions.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `120000`
- depends on: `basicly-ibzr0f`
- demonstration: Run a supervised pass while separately running work the engine did not dispatch, then read the board and check that nothing on it claims to be showing that second population - and if the design admits it, that it is drawn as something other than a lane.

## Steps to Reproduce

Run any agent without the supervisor - a bare claude session in this checkout, or `basicly loop run` before its worktree binds - then open the board: the lanes region names only records carrying a worktree external_ref, and `running now` counts more work than any visible lane, with nothing on the page saying the difference exists.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: The `running now` heading shall name only the population it actually draws, not implying it shows all running work. Whether a host subagent or a background job is observable by this engine at all shall be established and recorded with evidence. Where such work is observable and drawn, it shall be visually distinct from a lane and carry none of a lane's affordances.

## Trigger

When the board header shows a run id with no title, an unlabelled progress bar, a stale-looking gates cell, and lifetime machine spend on the run's own line, I want every header cell to carry a labelled figure, so I can read the header without tripping on any of its measured defects.

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-02: "header is still confusing." Third time the header is raised; basicly-jbd80w and basicly-v8jwf0 moved rows and fixed the alarm band, and the owner still cannot read it. This record states what the header holds today, so the next change is against a measurement and not a feeling.

Measured on the live page at 1712x1345, three lines left and one cell right:

```text
basicly  REPO basicly · main · 1687bc87   RUN basicly-k6tpep · open · L3 [bar] 43%
GATES [GREEN] mode full · recorded 2026-09-01T19:38:28Z   SPEND machine-local · 2,032.19 usd · 36.59 usd largest · 1.4B in · 8.7M out
CLOSED TODAY not measured
                                   as of 11s ago / 2026-09-02T09:18:28Z · stale after 60s · [●] producer basicly · 0.11.0
```

Seven things a reader trips on, each verifiable against the snapshot:

1. `RUN basicly-k6tpep` is an id with no title. The snapshot's `units[]` holds the root's title; the header does not use it.
2. `L3 [bar] 43%` names no figure and no denominator. `session.spent_tokens` 42,966,175 of `token_budget` 100,000,000, and `spent_tokens_live` 55,722,904 already reads higher than the committed figure the bar uses.
3. `GATES GREEN` beside `recorded 2026-09-01T19:38:28Z` says the green is yesterday's, and nothing says whether that is fine.
4. `SPEND machine-local · 2,032.19 usd` is the lifetime spend of this machine, not the run's. It sits on the run's line and reads as the run's cost.
5. `1.4B in · 8.7M out` are lifetime token counts with no reader action attached.
6. `CLOSED TODAY not measured` is a standing row that says nothing, the shape basicly-ibzr0f removed from the cards.
7. The right cell repeats the time three ways (`as of 11s ago`, the timestamp, `stale after 60s`) and carries the boxed glyph from the sibling record.

## Raised a fourth time, 2026-09-06

Owner, on the same header: *"another thing that i do not like is the header top right corner
banner. there we can improve the visualization."* That is defect 7 above, unchanged, and the
fourth session in which this header has been raised. Priority moved to P1 on that ground
alone: a complaint a person repeats four times is a requirement with no gate behind it.

Measured again on the 2026-09-06 wall, the same cell now reads:

```text
                    as of 2s ago
2026-09-06T14:39:36Z - stale after 60s - producer basicly - 0.11.0
```

Still three renderings of one instant, still boxed in green so it competes with the alarm band
directly beneath it, and still carrying the producer name and version - two facts no operator
acts on - in the wall's most valuable corner.

Two figures on the left have moved since this was filed. The grant bar now reads `103%` with
no numerator and no denominator, which is defect 2 having crossed its own budget. And
`CLOSED TODAY 4` finally measures something, which retires defect 6.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `src/basicly/board_render.py`
- `src/basicly/board_footer.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_regions.py`
- `tests/test_board_render.py`
- `tests/test_board_footer.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `70000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: render the wall and read the header aloud - every figure has a denominator, every id has a title, and the right cell states the instant once.

## Earlier acceptance text (the acceptance field is authoritative)

- WHEN the header renders, LINE ONE SHALL answer which checkout and which run: repo, branch, short head, the root's title with its id beside it, and the run status.
- WHEN a grant is live, THE HEADER SHALL print `spent of budget tokens` as two figures with the bar, using the live figure where the producer holds one and naming the committed figure as such otherwise.
- WHEN the gates cell renders, IT SHALL carry the verdict and the age of the record in the same phrase form as freshness (`recorded 14h ago`), and SHALL colour amber past the same stale threshold the freshness cell uses.
- Lifetime spend and lifetime token counts SHALL move to the footer beside `agents`, and the header SHALL carry the run's own spend only.
- A header cell whose value is `not measured` SHALL NOT render; the absence SHALL appear in the `not drawn` inventory only.
- THE freshness cell SHALL state the time once as `as of 11s ago`, keep the stale threshold, and drop the timestamp to a `title` attribute.
- `tests/test_board_render.py` SHALL assert the header cell order and the absence of `not measured` cells on the fixture.

Assumption stated: the owner named no specific confusion, so the seven items above are the ones measured on the page. The owner may strike or add items before this is dispatched.

When three assumptions carry large downstream decisions and each has a cheap test, I want each measured with its number, method and date on the record that owns it, so I can decide the expensive phases from data rather than argument.

## Trigger

When a third-party claim says that conditional-relevance blocks improve an agent's adherence to guidance, I want our own recall-eval instrument to measure the adherence difference on this catalog, so I can decide whether to adopt the mechanism from evidence rather than the claim alone.

## Context

`humanlayer/skills` `improve-claude-md` (**MIT**) claims Claude Code's system reminder -
this context may or may not be relevant - makes the model ignore parts of a CLAUDE.md, and
proposes wrapping conditional guidance in `<important if="condition">` blocks.

## Why this is ours to test and not to assume

We measured **recall**: 98% claude, 93% copilot (`basicly-agzx.1`). Their claim is about
**adherence**. Those are different quantities, and this repo's own standing rule is that
recall is an upper bound that may not be cited as evidence of quality. So our data neither
supports nor refutes them, and we have the instrument - `.scripts/recall_eval.py` plus the
path-scoped tier - that would settle it.

## Two constraints on the answer

1. **Claude root only.** `<important if>` is Claude-specific XML, and `basicly-a3ab.5`
   forbids one target's instruction file naming another target's enforcement mechanism. If
   it wins it becomes a projection detail in `.claude/rules/`, never `AGENTS.md`.
2. **The premise is an assertion about a vendor's internals.** Per the `interface-facts`
   rule, check the vendor's current documentation for what it says about instruction
   weighting before attributing a mechanism to the result. A measured difference with no
   explanation is still a finding; a claimed mechanism is not.

## Also adopt regardless of the outcome

Two portable rules from the same source, neither Claude-specific: cut any instruction a gate
can enforce, and cut code snippets in favour of file-path references. Both belong in
`basicly-a3ab.1`'s baseline audit.

## Scope

- `.scripts/recall_eval.py`
- `.basicly/core/fragments/**`
- `tests/**`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `90000`
- depends on: none

## Trigger

When a prompter names a concrete model that a host cannot run, I want the spawn to fall back to the same-tier model the host does support, so I can honour the intent behind the request instead of failing it outright.

## Context

Owner requirement 2026-07-31. A human prompter writes something like "spawn an agent that uses
gpt-5.6 sol and send it to analyze this document". The expectation: on copilot it succeeds literally,
because copilot serves that model; on claude it cannot, so it should fall back to the model of the SAME
TIER that the host can actually run. This is the reverse of basicly-kjc5.61's forward lookup and needs
its own mechanism plus catalog guidance, because the agent acting on the request is the thing that has
to do the resolving.

Verified constraint: **claude code cannot run a GPT model at all.** Its subagent `model` field accepts
`sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`, a full claude model id, or `inherit` - every value is Anthropic. So
a literal cross-vendor request is impossible there and substitution is the only non-failing option.
Copilot by contrast serves 6 vendors (measured: 29 models spanning OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft,
Moonshot AI, xAI), so it can honour most such requests literally.

## The sharp problem: reverse lookup is AMBIGUOUS

In the anchor set, `gpt-5.6-sol` occupies BOTH `high` and `maximum`, because OpenAI ships a three-class
ladder and the top class serves both tiers (docs/design/agent-roster-design.md R5). So resolving
"sol" backwards yields two tiers, and on claude they substitute differently: `high` gives
`claude-opus-5`, `maximum` gives `claude-fable-5` - which is double the input price and five times the
output price. A naive implementation picks whichever row it hits first and no one notices.

The same collapse applies to Moonshot (`kimi-k3`) and Google (`gemini-3.1-pro-preview`) in the derived
map, so this is the normal case, not an edge case.

## Two hard rules, both inherited from existing decisions

1. **Substitution must be VISIBLE.** If the prompter asked for `gpt-5.6-sol` and the agent spawns on
   `claude-opus-5`, that must be stated back to the prompter. basicly-kjc5.59 already establishes
   "record that the tier was not honoured rather than implying it was"; this is the same rule at the
   prompt surface. An invisible model swap is worse than a refusal because the prompter believes the
   request was honoured.
2. **An ambiguous reverse lookup is resolved by a documented rule or REFUSED, never guessed.** Options
   worth weighing: prefer the lowest tier that maps to the named model (cheapest, least surprising, and
   errs toward not overspending); or refuse and ask which tier was meant. Fail closed either way -
   "cannot tell" must never read as "safe to proceed". Whatever is chosen must be written down.

## Delivery shape

Per the owner, this needs distributing as guidance, not only as engine code: instructions and/or a skill
that teach an agent to (a) recognise a prompt naming a concrete model, (b) resolve it through the
committed map, (c) substitute tier-preserving where the host cannot honour it, and (d) say what it did.
It must work for custom agents and ad-hoc prompts, not just catalog-shipped agents - so it pairs with
basicly-wbsz's no-harness-required kit.

Mind the always-on budget: the baseline is at its soft cap, so this belongs in a skill or a path-scoped
fragment, not another `applies_to: [all]` fragment (see basicly-a3ab.1 and the headroom table in
docs/architecture/architecture.md section 7).

Depends on basicly-kjc5.61 for the map. Related: basicly-izda (ordered preference lists),
basicly-wbsz (portable kit), basicly-a3yi (emission), basicly-5xcj (tier-choice guidance, which this
should not duplicate).

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: When a prompt names a model the current host cannot run, the agent shall spawn on the same-tier model the host does support, and shall report the substitution naming both the requested and the actual model. When a named model's reverse lookup maps to more than one tier, the documented disambiguation rule (interactive: ask; non-interactive: price parity, then task class, then higher tier as last resort) shall apply, or the request shall be refused rather than a tier being guessed.

## Trigger

When `decompose._quantile_high` and `tuning._quantile` implement the identical algorithm as two separate copies with no test binding them, I want a test asserting they agree, so I can catch a silent divergence between the recommended bound and the enforced one.

## Context

Found by the lane-D measurement survey 2026-08-14.

```text
decompose._quantile_high   decompose.py:1425-1440
tuning._quantile           tuning.py:365-375
```

The two bodies are the same algorithm character for character: `index = math.ceil(quantile * len(ordered)) - 1`, a clamp, and the observed-sample rule. `tuning.py:369-371` states the duplication is deliberate, because `tuning` sits above `decompose` in the declared tiers.

## The specific risk

`tuning` recommends values for the working-set maximum and the ceiling with its copy. `decompose` enforces the unsized bound with the other. If one is edited, for example to interpolate, then the recommendation and the enforcement diverge in silence. That is the context-ceiling failure shape this repository already paid for. No test asserts the two agree.

## The fix is a test, not a refactor

Do not move the function to satisfy a layering preference. A ten-line statistics module at the bottom tier costs more than the test.

## Scope

- `tests/test_tuning.py`

## Depends on

The extraction of the spend forecast out of `decompose`, which moves `_quantile_high`. Write the test against its new home.

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_tuning.py -q`.

payload.name: requirements
payload.value: A test shall assert the two quantile functions return equal values over a shared sample table. The sample table shall include a single-element input, both extreme quantiles, and tied values.

When `board_regions.py` carries the running-lane region under a size waiver because extracting it would race a concurrent edit to .importlinter, I want the region moved to its own module, so I can retire the waiver and bring the file back under its cap.

## Context

`basicly-gnpgf8` rewrote the board's layout and lane card and left `src/basicly/board_regions.py` at 4056 of its 4000-token cap. It shipped under a `cost()` waiver rather than a split, and this record is the debt.

## The cut exists and is nameable

`flight`, `_lane_cells` and `_phase_of` are one responsibility - the running-lane region - and they are the part that grew. They would move to `board_flight.py` cleanly; the region's data comes from one section of the document and nothing else in the module reads them.

The test split has already happened and proves the seam: `tests/test_board_regions_flight.py` was cut out of `tests/test_board_regions.py` in the same change, under the `test_<module>_<aspect>.py` convention this repo already uses for `test_board_regions_grouping.py`.

## Why it was not taken now

**Every one of the 116 modules under `src/basicly/` is named in `.importlinter`'s layer list**, so a new module needs a line there, and that file is declared scope of `basicly-rn0o.6` - committed and unlanded, with an agent inside its worktree when this was written. Editing it from a second worktree races a landing.

This is the second time today the same block produced the same waiver; the first is `basicly-0bj8q1` on `board_facts.py`. Two instances of one cause is worth saying plainly: **the layer contract naming every module makes any extraction contend with whoever holds that file**, which is the opposite of what a size ratchet is trying to encourage.

Prose was cut first and was not enough - the remaining reasoning is about which tier holds which fact and why a row is absent, which is the content the cap exists to protect rather than narration.

1. `uv run python .scripts/check_module_size.py`
2. `grep -n 'module-size-waiver' src/basicly/board_regions.py`

**Control.** `uv run python .scripts/check_waivers.py` passes while this record is open, and must fail once it closes with the waiver still in the file - that expiry is what makes this debt rather than an exemption.

## Trigger

When the R9 requirements-ladder row still claims `fsck.rebuild` is exempt from the shrink guard by construction, I want the row corrected to say the comparison runs before the unlink, so I can stop the architecture document asserting a gap the code already closed.

## Context

`docs/architecture/architecture.md:3018` — the R9 row of the requirements ladder — ends with:

> **One path is exempt by construction:** `fsck.rebuild` unlinks the target before writing, so the guard always meets an absent file and the rebuild that loses records is the one it cannot see

The code refutes it. `basicly-dx2ngn` closed that hole, and the fix carries its own comment saying so.

## Measured

`.basicly/core/kit/tracker/fsck.py:953-962`:

```python
    # Derived and compared before anything is deleted (basicly-dx2ngn). `write_snapshot`'s
    # shrink guard compares against the file on disk and the unlink below guarantees there is
    # none, so R9's refusal could never fire through this path. Taking it after the unlink
    # would destroy the records it exists to keep, so a refused rebuild removes nothing.
    produced = tuple((path, derive(covered)) for path, covered in derived_targets(ledger))
    for path, proposed in produced:
        loss = snapshot.shrinkage(path, proposed)
        if loss.refused:
            raise snapshot.SnapshotError(f"{path.name}: {loss.reason}")
    removed = tuple(snapshot.derived_paths(ledger))
```

The comparison happens **before** the unlink loop, and `tests/test_kit_tracker_fsck.py:832` asserts the refusal fires with `"0 records over a file holding 2"`.

So the ladder's most load-bearing row tells a reader the one gap that is closed is open. Found by the `curator` at `basicly-b2n2`'s ship, and confirmed against the code.

## Scope

- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `tests/test_docs_claims.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L1`
- demonstration: Read the R9 row against `fsck.py:953-962` and the test at `test_kit_tracker_fsck.py:832`.

## Trigger

When a repository declares `[[privacy.denied]]` tokens locally and scrub_ledger rewrites the whole ledger without redacting them, I want the scrub to replace those tokens the same way it replaces machine identity, so I can commit without internal-info-scan refusing old payloads it re-presents as new lines.

## Context

Found 2026-09-01 while committing tracker state. tracker.scrub_ledger repairs what tracker-path-scan refuses (machine identity and paths, via redact.redact_committed), but internal-info-scan refuses a disjoint token set ([[privacy.denied]] in basicly.local.toml). scrub_ledger re-mints every rewritten line, internal-info-scan reads added lines only, so any whole-file scrub re-presents old payloads carrying a denied token as new lines and the commit is blocked with no engine repair.
